Not only did I accept the offer, but I also asked to meet the team first.
Never have I joined a company with such a strong finance team.
Only when I have met each of you will I talk about changes.
At no point will you hear about a decision from somebody else first.
Not only is this a strong team, but it is also a team that closes on time.
Welcome, Fernando. I hope the onboarding has not been all paperwork.
Not all of it. But never have I signed so many forms before lunch.
That is the security team, I am afraid. So, where would you like to start?
With you. I have read the handover notes, but I would rather hear it from you. What slows the team down?
Honestly, the month-end close. The bottleneck is the approvals from the regional offices. We lose two days every month waiting for them.
That is useful. And how is morale?
Not great. People work late at the end of every month, and nobody has asked them about it for a long time.
Then let me be clear about one thing. At no point will I change that process without talking to the people who run it.
That would be new. The team will want to hear it from you at the town hall on Thursday.
They will. And not only will I say it, but I will also come back in a month and show them what we did.
Never have I read a handover as clear as this one.
Give me a month to take stock, and then hold me to it.

When I hire a new finance chief, I tell them the same thing on the first morning. Under no circumstances do I expect a plan in the first week. In fact, I would be worried if I got one. Rarely does a new person understand a business in five days, however good they are. What I want instead is a list of questions. Who are the people I need to meet? Where does the money really come from? Which processes does the team complain about? Only when those questions have answers do I want to talk about changes. The best finance chief I ever hired spent his whole first month in meetings, and at no point did he ask me for more time.

My first town hall as a finance director was a disaster, and I still remember every minute of it. I had been in the job for three days. I stood up in front of eighty people and presented five changes to the month-end close. Never have I seen a room go so quiet. Nobody asked a single question. Later, my controller told me why: the team had built that process themselves, and they heard about my changes at the same time as everyone else. In my next job, I did it differently. Not only did I wait a month before the first town hall, but I also met every team leader first. The changes were almost the same. This time, people asked when we could start.

On Monday, Fernando arrives for his onboarding and meets the chief executive. Next, he reads the handover notes from the interim CFO. In a one-to-one, Beatriz tells him about the bottleneck in the month-end close. At the town hall on Thursday, he says that only when he has taken stock will he talk about changes. Finally, he promises to come back in a month and show the team what they did.
